subject: The 30-Second Email Test
challenge: Open an email you need to reply to. Click the Copilot button in Outlook and let it draft a response. Don't send it yet — just read what it wrote. How close was it to what you would have said? Now try option two: write a rough dot-point reply yourself, then ask Copilot to polish it. Which result sounds more like you? That difference is worth noticing.
teaching: Let Copilot draft a reply to a student query about an assignment, then try giving it your rough notes to work from. Which version captures your tone and the nuance of what you actually mean?
research: Let Copilot draft a reply to a collaborator's email about a paper revision both ways — from scratch, then from your rough points. Does starting with your words keep the disciplinary context that AI flattens into generic academic-speak?
professional: Let Copilot draft a reply to an internal request both ways — from nothing, then from your dot points. For routine emails, which approach needs less editing?

subject: Make Copilot Explain Your Job
challenge: Open Copilot chat and type: 'Explain what a [your job title] at a university does, as if you're telling a curious 10-year-old.' Then try: 'Now focus on the parts that would surprise people.' Share the funniest line with a colleague.
teaching: Ask Copilot to explain what a unit coordinator actually does. Does it mention the 47 emails before 9am? The pastoral care nobody trained you for?
research: Ask Copilot to explain what a research fellow does. See if it grasps the grant-writing treadmill or just says 'advances human knowledge.'
professional: Ask Copilot to explain your role. Professional staff roles are often invisible in universities — see how well AI understands what you actually do versus your position description.

subject: The Two-Chat Workflow
challenge: Next time you need AI help with something real, use two separate chat sessions. Session 1 is your Thinking Chat: explore, challenge assumptions, follow tangents, clarify what your actual question is. This is messy by design. Its purpose is to sharpen your thinking, not produce output. Then stop. Read through what emerged. Decide what matters. Discard what doesn't. Decide what you'll carry across. Write a focused brief. Session 2 is your Build Chat: produce the actual output using that brief. Keep flipping between the two sessions as needed. The magic is what happens between the two. You don't copy-paste from session one to session two. That curation, deciding what crosses from thinking to building, is where your judgement lives. Neither session has the full picture. Only you hold both. That's the real meaning of 'human in the loop.'
teaching: You are designing a new assessment task. Chat 1: brainstorm with AI about what skills you want to test, what has gone wrong before, what students struggle with. When you feel your thinking has sharpened, write a one-paragraph brief. Chat 2: draft the task sheet from that brief. The assessment will be sharper because you thought before you built.
research: You are drafting a grant application. Chat 1: explore the research gap, test your framing, challenge your assumptions about significance. When something clicks, distil your argument into a clear brief. Chat 2: write the actual section.
professional: You need to write a process document or proposal. Chat 1: talk through the problem, surface edge cases, clarify who the audience is. When you know what you're trying to say, write a focused brief. Chat 2: produce the document. You will notice the output is better because the thinking was done first.

subject: Your Meeting in 60 Seconds
challenge: After your next Teams meeting, ask Copilot to summarise the key decisions and action items. That takes 10 seconds. Now here is the real challenge: ask 'What decisions were implied but never actually stated?' then 'What questions were raised but not answered?' and 'What was discussed but not resolved?' Compare those answers to what you walked away thinking. Did AI surface something you missed — or were you already ahead of it?
teaching: After a teaching team meeting, get the summary, then ask 'What curriculum decisions were implied but not explicitly agreed on?' and 'What student issues were mentioned but not followed up?' These are the things that resurface three weeks later when nobody remembers who was meant to act.
research: After a research group meeting, get the summary, then ask 'What assumptions about the methodology went unchallenged?' and 'What deadlines were implied but not confirmed?' Useful for keeping collaborators aligned on what was actually decided versus what felt decided.
professional: After any meeting, get the summary, then ask 'What was discussed but not resolved?' and 'What actions were implied but not assigned to anyone?' Back-to-back meeting days are where things fall through the cracks — this is how you catch them.

subject: Who Gets the Credit?
challenge: You use Copilot to help write a funding application. The structure is yours, the data is yours, but Copilot polished the prose and suggested two paragraphs you kept almost unchanged. Should you disclose the AI assistance?
teaching: If a student used AI the same way you just did on that funding application, would you consider it academic misconduct? Whatever your answer, make sure your policy matches your own practice.
research: Check your target journal's AI policy. Some require disclosure, others prohibit AI-generated text entirely. Curtin's research guidelines are evolving too. Better to know before you submit.
professional: You draft a board paper and Copilot restructures your argument. Nobody asks who helped. Should they? Professional staff use AI for writing constantly — the norms are being set right now by what we normalise.

subject: Offloading or Surrendering?
concept: Keep your thinking in the loop
challenge: There's a useful difference between two ways we use AI. Cognitive offloading is strategic: you delegate a task (a calculation, a draft, a summary) but you stay in charge, you check the output, you'd notice if it were wrong. Cognitive surrender is when you stop checking. The answer looks fluent, sounds confident, and you accept it as your own. Pick one AI interaction from this week. Ask yourself honestly: would I have noticed if it were wrong? If the answer is no, that one's worth a second look. (Psychologists call the deliberate-checking mode System 2. The trick is making sure it still shows up to work.)
teaching: You ask Copilot to generate discussion questions for next week's tutorial. Offloading: you read them, cut the two that won't land with this cohort, and rewrite one that's subtly loaded. Surrender: you paste them into the slides. You'll find out which you did about ninety seconds into the tutorial.
research: You ask Copilot to summarise a paper for your literature review. Offloading: you skim the original to check the summary didn't flatten a key nuance. Surrender: you cite the summary. The difference matters when a reviewer asks a pointed question.
professional: You ask Copilot to draft a response to a tricky email. Offloading: you read it, notice it's slightly too formal for this colleague, and adjust. Surrender: you hit send. Most of the time it's fine. The one time it isn't is the one you'll remember.

subject: Copilot Lives in Word
challenge: Open a Word document you're working on. Highlight a paragraph and ask Copilot to 'make this more concise' or 'change the tone to formal.' You just edited with AI without leaving Word.
teaching: Paste your draft unit outline into Word. Ask Copilot to 'simplify the language for first-year students' or 'check this for jargon.' It refines your voice rather than replacing it.
research: Paste a rough abstract or grant section. Ask Copilot to 'tighten this to 250 words' or 'make the significance statement stronger.' Starting with your draft means the output sounds like you.
professional: Paste a process document or policy draft. Ask Copilot to 'make this clearer for someone new to the university' or 'convert this into dot points.' Great for onboarding documents.

subject: The 25-Word Test
concept: If you can't say it in 25 words the thinking isn't done
challenge: Take something you've asked Copilot to help with this week. Add a word constraint to your next request: 'Summarise the main argument in exactly 25 words' or 'State the key recommendation in 20 words or fewer.' Read what comes back. If the result is vague or padded, that's unclear thinking exposed, not hidden. The constraint is a diagnostic. It doesn't improve the output by magic — it removes the places where fuzzy thinking usually hides.
teaching: Ask Copilot to summarise a learning outcome in 20 words. If it produces hedging or jargon, your outcome may not be as clear as you thought. Try rewriting it yourself under the same constraint. The 20-word version is often sharper than the original.
research: State your research gap in 30 words — not the background, not the context, just the gap. If Copilot produces a vague sentence, it is reflecting your framing back at you. If you can't tighten it, the argument needs more work before it goes into a paper or grant application.
professional: Ask Copilot to give you the key ask of a long document in one sentence, 15 words maximum. If it hedges, the document probably hedges too. Useful before sending anything to a senior stakeholder who will not read past the first paragraph.

subject: The Be Specific Experiment
challenge: Ask Copilot: 'Give me some ideas for a workshop.' Then try: 'Give me five interactive workshop activities for university staff who have never used AI, each should take under 10 minutes and require no preparation.' Compare the two responses.
teaching: Try a vague prompt: 'Help me with my lecture.' Then try: 'I teach second-year marketing to 120 students. Suggest three ways to open next week's lecture on consumer behaviour that will get them talking in the first 5 minutes.' Night and day.
research: Try: 'Help me with my literature review.' Then: 'I'm reviewing qualitative studies on academic resilience published between 2020–2025. Suggest a thematic structure for organising 30 papers.' Specificity is everything.
professional: Try: 'Help me write a report.' Then: 'I need a one-page summary of semester 1 student complaints for the Associate Dean, highlighting the three most common themes and any trends compared to last year.' See the difference?

subject: Tame Your Spreadsheet
concept: Match the tool to the task
challenge: Open an Excel file you use regularly. Click the Copilot button and ask: 'What trends do you see in this data?' or 'Create a summary table of [column] by [category].'
teaching: Ask Copilot to analyse your grade distribution spreadsheet. 'Show me which assessments have the highest failure rates' or 'Compare average marks across tutorial groups.'
research: Ask Copilot to help with your research data. 'Suggest appropriate statistical tests for this dataset' or 'Create a summary table grouped by participant category.' Always verify its suggestions.
professional: Ask Copilot to analyse an operational spreadsheet — enrolment numbers, budget tracking, room bookings. 'What patterns do you see?' can surface things you'd miss scanning rows manually.

subject: Pass It On
challenge: Think of one colleague who might find these challenges useful. Send them a quick message: 'Hey, have you seen AI in 5? Worth a look.' That is this week's challenge.
teaching: Mention it at your next teaching team meeting. 'Has anyone tried the AI in 5 challenges?' Even one conversation can shift a team's willingness to experiment.
research: Mention it to a colleague in your research group or at your next HDR supervision. Research culture changes through trusted peer recommendations.
professional: Forward this email to someone in your team. Professional staff networks are tight — if you found something useful, chances are your colleagues will too.

subject: The Handover Prompt
challenge: Your chat with AI has been useful for an hour, but it's getting long, the thread is drifting, and you need to come back to it tomorrow. Try this: ask the AI to 'write a handover prompt that captures everything important from this conversation: context, decisions made, where we left off, so I can paste it into a new chat and continue.' Copy the result, save it somewhere (a note, a doc, an email to yourself), or leave it in the conversation, then start a fresh session and paste it in. You keep the thinking, you lose the noise.
teaching: Mid-semester unit redesign chat got tangled? Ask for a handover prompt before you lose the thread. Pick it up next week in a clean session without scrolling through forty messages.
research: Drafting a methods section over multiple sittings? End each session with a handover prompt. The next session starts sharp instead of you re-explaining what you'd already worked out.
professional: Working through a long policy draft or proposal with AI? When the chat gets too noisy to follow, generate a handover prompt and start fresh. Same context, less clutter.

subject: Give Copilot a Role
concept: A role narrows Copilot toward relevant knowledge and stance. The strongest roles give you a perspective you lack.
challenge: Try this in Copilot chat: 'You are an experienced academic developer at an Australian university. Review this learning outcome and suggest improvements: [paste one].' Then send the same request with no role. The version with a role is sharper because naming who Copilot speaks as narrows it toward the knowledge and tone that fit. The biggest gains come from roles that hand you a perspective you do not have yourself. (Role is the R in RTCF, the full prompt scaffold lives in the AI Toolkit.)
teaching: Try: 'You are a student encountering this unit for the first time. Read this assessment brief and tell me what confuses you.' Giving Copilot a student perspective can reveal blind spots in your instructions.
research: Try: 'You are a journal reviewer in [your field]. Review this abstract and identify weaknesses.' A role-based prompt produces feedback that is far more targeted than a generic request.
professional: Try: 'You are a new staff member on your first day. Read this onboarding document and list anything that is unclear or assumes prior knowledge.' Role prompts are powerful for testing whether your documents actually make sense.

subject: Bias Has Moved
challenge: Ask Copilot: 'Write a one-paragraph scene of a new academic on their first day at an Australian university.' Then in a fresh prompt: 'Write a one-paragraph scene of a new professional staff member on their first day.' Read them side by side. The interesting bias isn't whether one is a man and one a woman — frontier models have been trained hard against the obvious stereotypes. It lives in the smaller choices. What is each character called — 'Dr Chen' or 'Sarah'? What do they worry about? Whose office has the window? Who has authority in the scene? The story tells you what the model thinks each role looks like, and that picture does quiet work every time you use it.
teaching: Run the same exercise with 'a struggling first-year student' versus 'a high-achieving first-year student.' Notice the defaults — discipline, background, family situation, why they're struggling or succeeding. The model's assumptions are doing some of your pastoral thinking for you whether you noticed or not.
research: Try 'a brilliant early-career researcher' and 'a brilliant senior researcher.' What field? What kind of work? Whose career trajectory does the model treat as the default shape of success? If you use Copilot to help with reference letters or selection criteria, those defaults are leaking in.
professional: Try 'a respected senior manager' and 'a respected administrative officer.' Notice what changes — confidence, decisiveness, who's described as warm versus capable. If you draft position descriptions with Copilot, this is the air the document is breathing before you start editing.

subject: Summarise Before You Read
challenge: Find a long report or policy document you have been putting off. Paste it into Copilot chat: 'Summarise this in five bullet points and tell me what I should pay attention to.' Read the summary, then skim the original.
teaching: That 40-page curriculum review you've been avoiding? Copilot can give you the key points in 30 seconds. You still need to read the parts that matter — but now you know which parts matter.
research: That systematic review with 12,000 words? Ask Copilot to summarise the key findings and methodological approach. It won't replace critical reading, but it helps you triage a mountain of literature.
professional: That new university policy document that landed in your inbox? Summarise it first, then read the sections relevant to your area. You'll get through your reading pile in half the time.

subject: The Follow-Up Question
concept: Iteration is where the value lives
challenge: Most people ask Copilot one question and stop. Try a conversation: ask something, then follow up with 'Can you go deeper on point 2?' then 'What am I missing?' Three turns gets you from generic to genuinely useful.
teaching: Ask Copilot to suggest assessment ideas. Take the best one and say 'How would I scaffold this across weeks 3 to 10?' Then: 'What could go wrong with this approach?' The third answer is usually the most valuable.
research: Ask Copilot to help frame a research question. Then: 'What theoretical frameworks would support this?' Then: 'What would a reviewer say is missing?' Each turn sharpens the thinking.
professional: Ask Copilot to draft a process improvement proposal. Then: 'What objections will my manager raise?' Then: 'How do I address the budget concern?' This is conversation, not delegation.

subject: Your Top Tip
concept: Learning with AI is still learning
challenge: Fifteen weeks of AI in 5. What is the single most useful thing you have discovered? Reply with your tip — one sentence is plenty. We will compile the best into a Tips from Colleagues resource.
teaching: What changed in your teaching practice? Even a small shift — a better prompt, a new way to give feedback, a time-saving trick — is worth sharing with your teaching team.
research: What changed in your research workflow? Whether it saved you time, improved your writing, or just made you think differently about a tool, your experience helps others in your discipline.
professional: What changed in your day-to-day work? Professional staff tips are often the most practical and immediately applicable. Your colleagues want to hear what actually worked.

subject: PowerPoint in Five Minutes
challenge: Open PowerPoint, click Copilot, and type: 'Create a presentation about [your next talk topic].' Let it generate slides. Then refine: 'Add a slide comparing X and Y' or 'Make the title slide more engaging.'
teaching: Get Copilot to draft slides for your next lecture. The structure will need work, but it gives you something to react to rather than starting from a blank screen. Reaction is faster than creation.
research: Draft a conference presentation. Copilot's first attempt will be generic — but ask it to 'add more detail on methodology' or 'include a limitations slide' and it becomes a useful scaffold.
professional: Draft slides for a team update or committee report. Professional staff present more than people realise. A five-minute head start on a deck you were dreading is a genuine win.

subject: Verify Before You Trust
challenge: Next time AI gives you a fact, a statistic, a citation, or a confident claim, pause and ask yourself: 'How would I verify this?' You can't verify everything (you don't have time). Noticing when you should is half the skill. Pick one AI output this week and actually do the check. What did you find?
teaching: If Copilot cites a learning theory, references a paper, or quotes a curriculum framework, check it exists before you put it in front of students. Hallucinated references are confident and convincing right up until a student asks where it came from.
research: Confirm AI-suggested citations are real before you use them. Search the DOI, find the journal, read the abstract. Fluent output is not the same as accurate output, and a reviewer will notice a citation that does not exist.
professional: If AI quotes a policy, regulation, or procedure, check the wording at the source. Paraphrased confidence is not the same as the actual rule, and the difference can matter when someone acts on what you sent.

subject: When to Start Fresh
challenge: You've spent three messages trying to redirect a chat that's gone off track. Stop. Open a new session with a sharper prompt that captures what you've learned about what you actually want. You'll get a better result in less time than continuing to fight the old context. The chat is cheap, your time is not.
teaching: Quiz questions keep coming out too easy? New chat: 'Five short-answer questions at HD level for a third-year unit on X, requiring application not recall.' Faster than course-correcting six rounds of edits.
research: Stuck circling a research question? Start fresh with tighter constraints. The old chat is anchored to your first framing; the new one isn't. The reset is often where the breakthrough is.
professional: Tone of a draft email isn't landing? Start over, lead with the recipient relationship and your goal. Often quicker than five rounds of 'make it warmer / less formal / not like that.'

subject: The Two-Pass Workflow
challenge: After AI produces a draft, don't just edit it. Ask it to critique its own output: 'What are the weaknesses in this?' or 'What would a skeptical reader push back on?' Treat the first output as the start of the conversation, not the end. The second pass is where the value lives.
teaching: Drafted an assessment task? Ask 'What could a student exploit here?' or 'Where is this brief ambiguous?' The critique often surfaces things you'd otherwise discover only after submission day.
research: Drafted an abstract or grant section? Ask 'What would a reviewer say is missing or unclear?' Pre-empt the feedback before it costs you the round.
professional: Drafted a proposal or business case? Ask 'What objections will the budget holder raise?' Stronger document, fewer surprises in the meeting.
